title: Growth in private HE opens access but raises concerns
Three more international campuses set to open in Dubai
content:
Tweet
Three more international universities are set to open campuses in Dubai during the 2025 to 2026 academic year.
The universities will boost the 37 international branch campuses that already exist, which expand access to higher education but arguably have negligible impact on research and innovation, the core drivers of the knowledge-based economy.
This necessitates a shift toward enhancing investment in research capacity, academic-industry linkages, and evidence-driven policymaking, among others.
In a press release on 2 July, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA) announced that the universities confirmed to commence operations include the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad (IIM Ahmedabad), the American University of Beirut, and Saudi Arabia’s Fakeeh College for Medical Sciences. Additionally, the KHDA noted that discussions are ongoing with several other international universities.
Dr Wafi Dawood, CEO of the Strategic Development Sector at KHDA said: “This initiative aligns with the social and economic goals of the Dubai Economic Agenda D33 and the Education 33 Strategy , which represents a transformative vision for Dubai’s education system”.
The goal of the Education 33 Strategy’s global university attraction project is to establish a cutting-edge educational environment that combines national and transnational programmes that fund education, scientific research, and cross-border cooperation in a range of economic sectors.
According to KHDA, by 2033, 50% of students in the emirate’s higher education institutions will be foreigners, adding AED 5.6 billion (US$1.52 billion) to the gross domestic product (GDP) and placing Dubai among the top 10 locations in the world for university study.
“Our aim is to enhance the global competitiveness of Dubai’s graduates, increase educational tourism tenfold by 2033, integrate a new generation of Emiratis into the workforce and future sectors, and contribute to doubling Dubai’s economy over the next decade, positioning the city among the world’s top three economic hubs,” Dawood noted.
The UAE is currently ranked second among the top five hosting countries for foreign international campuses, after China and followed by Singapore, Malaysia, and Qatar, according to the March 2023 Branch Campus Listing prepared by the University of Miami’s Cross-Border Education Research Team (C-BERT).
Toward a more ‘multipolar TNE’
Dr Tim Rottleb at Brandenburg University of Technology Cottbus-Senftenberg in Germany, told University World News: “The opening of three new foreign campuses in Dubai highlights the city’s growing role as an emerging hub in the global landscape of transnational higher education (TNE).”
Rottleb, who is the author of the 2024 study “Offshore campus development and the worlding of Dubai as an international education hub”, noted that this indicates that traditional Western networks are losing their dominance over the international education market, which is becoming more diverse.
“The fact that these new campuses include institutions from outside the usual Anglo-American sphere shows how places like Dubai are actively cultivating new academic and economic ties,” he added.
He said this development suggests a shift toward a more multipolar TNE system, where new centres can emerge. “At the same time, it underscores the strategic ambitions of Dubai to position itself as a key node in these evolving global networks,” Rottleb pointed out.
Expanding access to HE
Professor Lokman Meho, based at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon, sees the addition of three new foreign campuses as a reflection of a strategic move by Dubai to expand access to higher education for nationals and, more importantly, key expatriate and neighbouring communities – Lebanese, Indian, and Saudi – within the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
While Dubai is currently ranked 72nd in the QS Best Student Cities 2025 rankings, it is, according to Meho, becoming a major host of international students through wisely investing in higher education institutions aligned with its D33 and E33 agendas to promote knowledge-based economic development.
“As a fast-growing, cosmopolitan city with a deep need for quality higher education, Dubai is moving fast on its ambition to be a Top 10 Student City,” Meho told University World News.
“These campuses will serve families who prefer to keep their children nearby, reduce the financial and logistical burdens of studying abroad, and respond to rising safety and visa concerns in traditional host countries,” he added. Andy Pacino , Director of Studies at EF Education First, has no doubt that the increase in the number of foreign campuses in Dubai contributes positively to the region’s HE landscape. According to Pacino, institutions like the University of Manchester and the University of Birmingham bring global expertise and advanced research capabilities to the region. “What they also offer is international collaboration that can foster and encourage innovation and human capital development,” he told University World News. Local vs satellite campuses However, Pacino highlighted the current rankings gap between local institutions and their foreign satellite campuses. “Not many branch campuses figure in either regional or international rankings, and local institutions are favoured rather than the satellite campuses. That could be put down to recent challenges in research output, integration with the local community, and visibility (or lack of it) of branch campus contributions,” Pacino explained. The home campuses of several foreign HE institutions with a presence in Dubai are ranked among the top 200 globally in the QS World University Rankings for 2026. These include the University of Manchester Dubai (35th), the University of Birmingham Dubai (76th), Curtin University Dubai (183rd), and the University of Wollongong Dubai (184th). In contrast, the 2024 local ranking for universities in the UAE identified only 4 foreign branch campuses, and the regional and international rankings have not included any foreign branch campuses. As University World News reported the list of 34 top research universities includes only four foreign branch campuses, namely New York University Abu Dhabi (group 1, outstanding), the University of Wollongong in Dubai (group 2, very good), and Sorbonne University-Abu Dhabi and Saint Joseph University-Dubai (group 3, good). The QS World University Rankings 2026 , and Arab university ranking (2024) have 12 public and private HE institutions but no foreign branch campus included. Negligible research impact “With the notable exception of NYU Abu Dhabi, which performs well on the Research Integrity Risk Index ( RI² ) and maintains a low research integrity-risk profile, most foreign branch campuses in the UAE, including those in Dubai, have had negligible research output or impact on the country’s academic landscape,” Meho noted. He said their primary focus has been on teaching and revenue generation rather than substantive research engagement. “This limited research activity constrains the applicability of RI² assessments to these institutions,” said Meho, who is the developer of the RI² – the world’s first empirically grounded, composite metric designed to identify and profile institutional-level risks to research integrity. “Whether the three newly announced campuses will follow the high-integrity, research-orientated model of NYU Abu Dhabi or align more closely with the largely teaching-focused profile of other foreign universities in the UAE remains to be seen.” Dubai’s foreign campuses are crucial to increasing access to higher education, particularly for its sizable and varied expatriate population, according to Meho. In addition, they minimise the financial and logistical burdens of studying abroad, promote global perspectives, and offer internationally accredited programmes – all of which should not be understated. “However, when it comes to research and innovation, that is, the core drivers of a true knowledge-based economy, their impact has been minimal. Despite the many foreign campuses in Dubai and the tens of thousands of students they enrol, they contribute to less than 25% of Dubai’s research output today,” Meho pointed out. “Realising Dubai’s D33 vision will ultimately require a shift toward deeper investment in research capacity, academic-industry linkages, and evidence-driven policymaking,” he concluded. Complex and uneven impact Rottleb is of the opinion that foreign campuses in Dubai promote knowledge-based economic development, but their impact is complex and uneven. “Branch campuses help Dubai strengthen its position as an emerging international education hub, diversifying transnational higher education beyond traditional Western centres. They meet demand for recognised degrees and supply skilled graduates to international companies operating locally,” he stated. “However, their contribution to building a truly local innovation ecosystem is limited.” He cautioned that even well-meaning institutions like KHDA, which genuinely seek to promote academic life and knowledge-based economy development, cannot fully overcome the boundaries set by the UAE’s authoritarian political climate, which restricts critical academic inquiry. Moreover, the majority of branch campus students – many of whom come from the resident migrant community in the United Arab Emirates – face residency insecurity and are focused on obtaining stable white-collar jobs or onward migration rather than long-term innovation-driven entrepreneurship. Research ambitions “Dubai’s model of hosting foreign universities in Free Zones has succeeded in attracting reputable global brands, including from non-Western countries. “But for branch campuses to move beyond being education service providers, there must be space for more open, critical academic engagement and attention to the social realities of the student population,” Rottleb pointed out. “While they supply qualified workers to international companies, genuine knowledge-based development also requires tackling the structural factors that currently limit local innovation capacity,” Rottleb suggested. For Rottleb, real knowledge-based development also requires tackling the structural factors that currently limit local innovation capacity, even as they supply qualified workers to international companies. Resultingly, branch campuses need to play a stronger role by being more integrated into local industry needs and national research priorities. “This means supporting joint research initiatives, incentivising collaboration with domestic universities, and investing in infrastructure for innovation. “Dubai also needs to offer incentives – particularly financial security – to encourage foreign universities to bring not only cash-cow teaching programmes but also research-intensive ones,” Rottleb explained. “Finally, attracting academics who conduct innovative research requires more than money: it demands creating an inspiring environment where people can think freely and critically engage with ideas,” he pointed out. Aligning branch and mother campuses Pacino argued that there could be stronger accreditation and quality assurances between foreign branches that (genuinely) align with mother campuses. In addition, there could be more promotion of regional partnerships with the industry’s bigger hitters, where they might create knowledge ecosystems to provide economic impacts such as workforce development and entrepreneurship. “Dubai’s strategic hub could benefit from a focus on policies that offer incentives to foreign campuses, not only to operate as a business, but to truly fulfil their customers’ (students’) needs with a holistic ecosystem that provides education and employment at the end of it,” Pacino said. Contributors to innovation For Meho, Dubai’s strategy to expand its higher education landscape through foreign branch campuses is commendable, particularly when it focuses on institutions that serve local needs while maintaining global standards. “However, for foreign campuses to truly add long-term value, Dubai must avoid becoming a haven for diploma mills or passive teaching outposts. The emphasis should be on establishing a reputation for academic integrity, research excellence, and societal and economic impact,” he cautioned. According to Meho, foreign branch campuses need to move beyond their current teaching-focused mandates and become active participants in the UAE’s research, innovation, and talent development ecosystems in order to better leverage branch campuses for economic development and fully align with Dubai's D33 and E33 agendas. A clear and intentional policy shift would be necessary for this transition, one that holds campuses accountable for their performance, promotes alignment with national strategic priorities, and incentivises meaningful research engagement. “Key recommendations include [adding] local relevance through mandating that branch campuses tailor academic programmes and research agendas to Dubai’s economic priorities, such as AI, healthcare, energy transition, and sustainability,” Meho suggested. Public-private partnerships through creating structured mechanisms for collaboration between campuses, industries, and government bodies to bridge the gap between education and workforce needs are also needed. In addition, accountability frameworks should be introduced that distinguish between teaching-only campuses and those contributing to knowledge production. Meho suggested that a shift of focus towards attracting research-intensive institutions, as Qatar did with Weill Cornell and Abu Dhabi did with NYU and Cleveland Clinic, is also needed. In order to raise branch campuses’ visibility and measure their influence, Meho proposed “ranking inclusion through advocating for the separate recognition and evaluation of branch campuses in regional and global university rankings”. He concluded: “Without such reforms, foreign campuses risk becoming passive educational outposts, but with them, they can become integral drivers of innovation, human capital development, and sustainable economic growth in Dubai.”

title: ‘Architect’ of flagship HE policy is nominated minister
content:
Tweet
The ‘architect’ of South Korea’s new president’s policy to have 10 major flagship universities in the country has been nominated as South Korea’s next minister of education under President Lee Jae-myung’s administration. Lee Jin-sook, former president of Chungnam National University, was nominated on 29 June.
Announcing the nomination, Chief Presidential Secretary Kang Hoon-sik said: “She was the first female president of Chungnam National University, her alma mater, and the first woman to lead a flagship national university in Korea.
She previously served as dean of the College of Engineering and as a member of the Presidential Advisory Council on Science and Technology.”
Lee chaired the policy team behind one of the president’s key campaign pledges: the ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ initiative to upgrade ten universities around the country to the level of the country’s most prestigious institution, Seoul National University (SNU).
“She was recommended numerous times through the public nomination system,” Kang noted, referring to a system set up by President Lee Jae-Myung last month where citizens can directly propose candidates for major public office.
The ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ policy was one of President Lee Jae-myung’s top ten pledges during his candidacy to replace impeached president Yoon Suk Yeol, who was removed after his declaration of martial law on 3 December 2024.
The flagship universities initiative proposes levelling up ten national universities across the country as a means to address educational inequality, ease university entrance pressures to get into the current few top universities in Seoul, and help reverse talent outflow from the regions.
“Support for flagship national universities will be expanded to a level comparable to SNU, allowing for the discovery of regional talent and enabling students to pursue master’s and doctoral degrees within their regions,” Lee said at a campaign rally in the southern city of Gwangju on 17 May.
The policy would involve a substantial boost in funding – particularly in per-student spending – and provision for collaboration with private universities and input from the education sector.
Currently, SNU spends about KRW60 million (US$43,800) per student, while those at other national universities receive just KRW25 million or less per student.
Lee’s education advisory team has proposed raising this amount to approximately 70% of the SNU level, according to party statements from 2024.
Chaired taskforce on flagship universities
Lee was officially appointed chair of the ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ task force within the Democratic Party’s central campaign committee in May 2025, just before the election.
At a press briefing in Daejeon on 29 May, she explained: “The idea of ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ has long been promoted by metropolitan and provincial superintendents (education officials), and when I suggested it to Lee Jae-myung’s campaign, it was enthusiastically adopted.
“It’s not just about creating elite regional universities – it’s about transforming the national education system and driving balanced development. I joined the campaign because I agreed with this vision.”
In 2020, Lee became the first woman in Chungnam National University’s 70-year history – and in any of Korea’s flagship national universities – to be elected president. Her election on 28 November 2019 was through a direct vote by faculty, students, and staff, reinforcing her democratic mandate. During her term, she pushed through academic reforms such as the establishment of a semiconductor-focused programme, laid the groundwork for a cross-regional campus model, and founded a new international studies division. In 2022, she served as chair of the National Council of Presidents of Public Universities. An architectural engineering professor by background, she also served as the chief urban architect for Daejeon city. Controversy over nomination However, Lee’s nomination as minister is not without controversy. On 4 July, the office of Kim Min-jeon, a member of the National Assembly’s Education Committee, raised concerns over potential research misconduct. In early 2018, while serving as a professor of architectural engineering, Lee published two papers just one month apart – one in the Journal of the Korean Society of Color Studies, and another in the Journal of Korean Institute of Illuminating and Electrical Installation Engineers. Both studies bore similar titles and conclusions, with experimental designs that overlapped substantially. The titles were: A Study on the Evaluation of Fatigue According to Area and Illuminance Variations in Lighting and A Study on the Evaluation of Discomfort Glare According to Area and Illuminance Variations in Lighting. The similarities led to accusations of ‘salami slicing’ – the practice of splitting one study into several publications. The experimental methodology in both papers was nearly identical. For instance, both state: “Eighteen students in their third year or higher from the Department of Architectural Engineering who were judged to possess perceptual ability in architectural lighting environments participated. “Subjects had no ophthalmological conditions such as colour blindness and had corrected vision of 1.0 or better.” These identical passages have attracted scrutiny from academic circles. A spokesperson from the Ministry of Education’s nomination hearing preparation team, responding to the allegations, said: “All of the candidate’s publications between 2007 and 2019 were reviewed by Chungnam National University’s research ethics committee during her appointment process, and no misconduct was found.” Upcoming confirmation hearing The official added other concerns would be addressed in the upcoming parliamentary committee confirmation hearing scheduled for 16 July. A key witness will be the head of Chungnam National University’s research ethics committee during her presidency, who is expected to testify on the allegations surrounding her publications. A senior official at the Ministry of Education told University World News: “If confirmed, Minister Lee is expected to accelerate implementation of the ‘Ten Seoul National Universities’ policy. We are hoping the hearing proceeds without major issues.” On 8 July, students from Lee’s laboratory released a public statement defending her. Signed collectively as members of the Environmental Planning Laboratory in the Department of Architectural Engineering, the statement read: “According to department regulations, degree theses must be based on articles listed in the Korea Citation Index (KCI). The overlapping content reported in the media stems from this academic procedure.” They added: “The articles misrepresenting the professor are deeply distressing. Professor Lee has always considered the growth of her students to be her greatest joy.” Controversy over overseas education A second controversy emerged this week, involving the education of Lee’s younger daughter. It was revealed that in 2007, the daughter enrolled in the ninth grade of an American middle school – equivalent to Korea’s Year 9 – before completing compulsory education in Korea. At the time, both Lee and her husband, a professor at Cheongju University, remained in Korea. Under South Korean law, compulsory education – including middle school – must be completed domestically unless a legal guardian accompanies the child abroad for unavoidable reasons. As of 2007, exemptions were granted only when all guardians left the country with the minor for cohabitation purposes. A breach of this provision carries a maximum administrative fine of 1 million won. At the time, Lee was serving as a professor at Chungnam National University’s School of Architectural Engineering, while also participating on government panels for the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, the Ministry of Knowledge Economy, and the Presidential Committee on Architecture Policy. Both she and her husband were residing in Korea and therefore failed to meet the legal requirements for authorised overseas study at the middle school level, according to experts. On 9 July, a spokesperson for the Education Ministry’s nomination hearing preparation team said: “Candidate Lee was not aware at the time that this constituted a legal violation. She only learnt of the issue recently and sincerely apologises to the public.” The spokesperson said: “All of the candidate’s publications between 2007 and 2019 were reviewed by Chungnam National University’s research ethics committee during her appointment process, and no misconduct was found.”

title: How do employers view the quality of HE and its graduates?
content:
Tweet
Employers considered the accreditation or recognition by a national professional body of an institution of higher learning, as well as its international ranking, as important factors in their decision-making about the employability of the institution’s graduates, a study in South Africa has revealed.
The study , captured in a recent report titled Stakeholder Perspectives on the Quality of Higher Education in South Africa, was prepared for the Council on Higher Education (CHE) by the South African Human Sciences Research Council.
The CHE publishes information about developments in higher education, including reports on the state of the sector, and promotes the access of students to higher education institutions, among other issues.
It aimed to investigate stakeholder perceptions of the quality of higher education. Overall, it surveyed three groups of participants: academic and management staff in public and private higher education institutions; current students and graduates; and private and public employers, employer organisations and external quality assurance bodies.
Employer sector
In the employer sector, 200 respondents from the government, community, social and personal services sectors were included. Also surveyed were those in the information and communications technology sphere; insurance, real estate and business services domain; and the manufacturing sector.
The largest proportion of respondents were human resources professionals, while there were several managers and senior professionals among the cohort.
“Performance of previous employees from that institution” was rated as important, although there was a greater spread in opinion in relation to this.
The study found that employer preferences “align with the … importance attached to compliance with norms and standards as a key measure of quality in higher education”.
What employers think about quality
The objective of the employer questionnaire was to determine what employers think is important for understanding and promoting quality in higher education. The survey questionnaire asked respondents to provide their views on higher education quality in relation to six composite measures:
•	Dimensions considered important for quality in higher education;
•	Graduate attributes to be developed through higher education;
•	Factors impacting on the decision to employ a graduate;
•	Important aspects of a university’s work in relation to its teaching, research and social responsibility functions;
•	Ways of assessing educational outcomes that are valued by employers; and •	Educational and recreational resources considered important for quality higher education. The institution you attend matters There was widespread agreement on the importance of the “institution that a graduate has attended” and the “reputation the institution has in South Africa among other employers”. External accreditation of the institution by international bodies was also important. The respondents unanimously acknowledged the importance of “socially and economically relevant and transformative” education as an indicator of quality with the importance of “personally transformative” education; education that is “accountable to stakeholders” and excellence and high standards in education, as other quality metrics. However, employers were comparatively less interested in value for money and appropriately resourced higher education as indicators of quality. Instead, they advised that higher education should focus on developing personal qualities in graduates such as self-esteem; personhood; recognition of the power of knowledge; self-discipline; and emotional stability and independence. The report indicated that employers “stressed the importance of developing cognitive and emotional attributes, including the capacity to reason and analytical skills”. There was also a sense that higher education should be making a social contribution; promote ethical awareness; and “produce graduates with a global perspective and a notion of citizenship”. Other institutional factors employers consider Other institutional factors that employers considered important in relation to employment decisions include institutional reputation in the context of histories of racism; sexual abuse or drug-related scandals and protests. “Staff achievements and the social contributions of institutions were also mentioned as critical factors,” according to the study. There was a high level of agreement on the importance of lecturers with teaching qualifications and lecturers who aim to transform attitudes and behaviours. There was more importance assigned by employers to lecturers having a teaching qualification as opposed to a PhD. “Employers clearly value lecturers’ exposure to pedagogy and content of the field they are teaching as opposed to a doctoral-level degree.” What about graduates’ grades? All those surveyed agreed on the importance of academic performance or high marks as a credible measure of assessing the outcomes of education, with 56.5% of participants rating this as “important” and 43.5% rating this as “very important”. There was also agreement on the importance of the other indicators for assessment. For example, continuous assessment to prepare students for their final assessments was rated as an effective way of measuring the quality of a graduate by 42.5% of the respondents. Similarly, “submission of documents, such as a CV and [a] qualification” was rated as important by 51% and as very important” by 42.5%. “There was an even greater unanimous acknowledgement of the importance of the indicator with the lowest mean score – assessment of academic knowledge – with 69.5% of respondents describing this indicator as important and the rest describing it as very important.” Educational resources and facilities Employers were asked to rate the importance of a number of educational and co-curricular resources and facilities as indicators of quality in higher education. The aspects which received the highest mean scores were financial support to students; cleanliness of campus and access to transport to and within the campus. The aspect which received the lowest mean score was student sports and sports facilities, even though most of the respondents rated the provision of such facilities as important. The respondents were less enthusiastic about the importance of student organisations and recreational facilities as an indicator of quality, although 60% noted that such provision was important. There was substantial agreement on the importance of a number of other educational and co-curricular resources and facilities as indicators of quality, including safety and security on campus; course materials and design; student instructional support; laboratories and other facilities; ICT, connectivity and computing and library resources. There was considerable agreement on the importance of online learning management systems; tutoring and small-group learning rooms; lecture halls; student health and psycho-social support; student residences; and number of students per class. “It is noteworthy that multilingualism was regarded as important by 54% of respondents and very important by 41%. While work experience from work-integrated learning, and job seeking and entrepreneurship skills were not selected by any employers as very important; the respondents generally viewed these attributes as either slightly important or important.” Positives and negatives In their consideration of various ways of measuring higher education outcomes, employers agreed unanimously on the importance of three main criteria: subject matter or academic knowledge; skills for the workplace and academic performance. Employers attached the greatest importance to knowledge and competence in the chosen degree or field of study. There was also almost unanimous support from employers for invigilated examinations as a test of knowledge and skills; alternative assessment methods (such as practicals and presentations) and continuous assessment. Employers indicated that “when hiring a graduate, the impression in a recruitment interview is more important than the grades”. The employer stakeholder group was critical about the (limited) extent of financial support (and the standard of the administration of funding) being offered to students; the quality of the social environment, social spaces and residences on campuses; the extent of the academic, counselling and mental health support provided to students; and the responsiveness of institutional governance processes in addressing student grievances. The stakeholders were generally positive in their assessment of change in the quality of higher education in democratic South Africa with respect to equity, expansion, diversity, and inclusion in higher education; the quality of academic staff and the involvement of academic staff in quality assurance, the study indicated. The employer stakeholder group recommended the fostering of collaboration between higher education institutions and employers, private industry and state-owned enterprises, local communities, community-based organisations and government and public entities, to align educational provision with societal and economic needs. The establishment of partnerships to support student skills development through initiatives such as industry placements, work-integrated learning, practicals, internships, and business incubation centres was also recommended.

title: When openness obscures power – Rethinking MOOCs
content:
Tweet
In the global rush to digitise learning, the word ‘open’ has become synonymous with progress. But not all openness is created equal.
Massive open online courses (MOOCs) have been celebrated as democratising forces, breaking down educational barriers and expanding access worldwide. Yet beneath the appealing rhetoric lies a more complex and more troubling reality.
MOOCs are not the same as open-access learning. They are platformised, proprietary, and often aligned more with profit than pedagogy.
The mirage of MOOC openness
When MOOCs were launched in the early 2010s by institutions like Stanford, MIT, and Harvard, they promised a revolution in global education.
Platforms like Coursera, edX, and FutureLearn offered free courses from top-tier universities, using the language of access, inclusion, and global empowerment. Millions enrolled, governments signed on, and the hype cycle surged.
But the model evolved rapidly into a commercial ecosystem. Courses became ‘freemium’, certificates came with a cost, and platform algorithms optimised engagement for monetisation.
A 2024 study published in Open Praxis analysed MOOCs on the Bilge portal and also noted persistently low completion rates, even after adjusting for engagement. This contextualises past findings and confirms that dropout remains a core issue in MOOCs.
Another study examined 2.3 million learners across 174 MITx courses, Open Praxis . The authors concluded that MOOCs continue to attract learners who are disproportionately older, male, and highly educated, indicating that those who least need open access education often benefit most.
Platform capitalism and data extraction
Today’s MOOCs operate under the logic of platform capitalism. Their governance is centralised, their content is institutionally curated, and their design prioritises scalability and data-driven personalisation over critical engagement.
Behavioural data is mined to enhance stickiness and convert users into paying customers, echoing the broader patterns of surveillance capitalism .
MOOCs promise global learning but often deliver digital franchising. The platforms act more like SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) companies than educational commons.
The knowledge offered is typically Western, English-language, and linear, with limited adaptability for local contexts. Instead of transforming learning, they simulate the traditional classroom on a digital interface.
MOOCs export knowledge – But seldom import context
MOOCs frequently export Western knowledge without meaningful local context, reinforcing patterns of digital neocolonialism. Their epistemic orientation favours Anglo-American paradigms, reinforcing a form of digital neocolonialism. Scholars such as Walter Mignolo have called this the “coloniality of knowledge”.
Courses on global development, education, or health are frequently written from elite Global North perspectives, with minimal representation of Global South voices or Indigenous knowledge systems. As a result, learners are socialised into accepting one way of knowing, while local traditions are sidelined or omitted entirely. Language is another barrier. Over 80% of MOOCs are offered in English , excluding millions of learners across the Global South who lack high-level proficiency. Even in multilingual initiatives like SWAYAM (India) or FUN MOOC (France), the pedagogy often mirrors colonial-era models – top-down, exam-driven, and institutionally guarded. What true open access learning looks like In contrast to MOOCs, open-access learning emphasises community, flexibility, and cultural relevance. Rooted in the tradition of knowledge commons, it is marked by community-led curriculum design, multilingual resources, open licensing, and peer-to-peer pedagogy. It values learner agency over credential scalability. Consider: The African Storybook Project : enables communities to develop and translate children’s books into local languages. Refugee-led coding academies in Lebanon : teaching Python through oral storytelling, blending tech with cultural narratives. Latin American women’s cooperatives : developing digital literacy tools from the ground up. These are not MOOCs. They are not massive. But they are open in the deepest sense: participatory, situated, and emancipatory. Case studies from four continents National MOOC platforms across the globe have adopted distinct strategies to expand access and assert cultural influence. While they differ in form and intention, a common thread runs through their designs: each platform reflects not only a pedagogical model but also a political project – embedding specific values, epistemologies, and power relations into digital learning. FutureLearn (United Kingdom): Cultural diplomacy through MOOCs Founded by the Open University and supported by the United Kingdom government, FutureLearn has actively positioned itself as a soft power instrument . Its initiatives include offering free courses to Afghan women and Ukrainian students during moments of political crisis, framed explicitly as part of broader public diplomacy efforts. These efforts extend Britain’s historical educational outreach, particularly in regions with colonial-era ties. UK universities partner through the platform to deliver English-language instruction and cultural curricula, reinforcing British influence under the banner of inclusion and humanitarian support. While access is broadened, the epistemic orientation remains largely Anglocentric. SWAYAM (India): Infrastructure without pedagogical transformation India’s SWAYAM platform (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) was launched by the Ministry of Education to provide free, multilingual online courses from Indian universities. It represents a commendable effort to build national digital infrastructure and reduce dependency on foreign edtech platforms. However, SWAYAM’s pedagogy remains deeply traditional, lecture-based, exam-driven, and focused on institutional authority. While it expands access, the platform’s hidden curriculum emphasises standardised success and individual merit, often marginalising critical pedagogy, learner agency, and cultural plurality. As a result, SWAYAM preserves rather than transforms prevailing educational hierarchies. FUN MOOC (France): Linguistic sovereignty and neo-republican education Launched in 2013 by the French Ministry of Higher Education, France Université Numérique ( FUN MOOC ) explicitly promotes Francophone education as a form of global cultural outreach. The platform has deepened ties with former French colonies, particularly through the Francophonie agenda – such as initiatives ahead of the 2024 Villers Cotterêts Summit , and by rolling out localised versions in countries like Morocco and Côte d’Ivoire. Though its pedagogy often mirrors the centralised, lecture-heavy model of France’s higher education system, FUN MOOC carries a clear decolonising impulse: it prioritises linguistic sovereignty and cultural continuity in the Francophone world. Yet, it stops short of embracing participatory learning or epistemic plurality, reflecting a neo-republican model of top-down educational dissemination. Coursera and edX (United States): Market logics and the coloniality of knowledge US-based MOOC platforms like Coursera and edX (now part of 2U) commercialise elite education at scale, distributing content from institutions such as Stanford and MIT to a global audience. Backed by Silicon Valley and academic prestige, they promote a hidden curriculum rooted in neoliberal values – self-optimisation, market alignment, and entrepreneurialism. Learners are framed as individual upskillers in gamified environments, with critical inquiry sidelined. Most content reflects Anglo-American epistemologies, often excluding Global South or Indigenous perspectives. This reinforces what decolonial scholars call the coloniality of knowledge, where power over learning remains concentrated in the Global North. The hidden curriculum: What MOOCs really teach The case studies above illuminate a deeper structural tension: while national MOOC initiatives have succeeded in broadening access and localising content to varying degrees, their true impact hinges less on technical infrastructure and more on the degree of epistemic autonomy they afford. The central question is not merely what MOOCs deliver, but how they structure the act of learning itself. Beneath the surface of open access lies a hidden curriculum, one that transmits the cultural logics of self-optimisation, competition, and credentialism. Learning is reframed as a solitary race toward certification, gamified into metrics and milestones. Reflection gives way to retention; transformation is replaced by task completion. Dialogue, where it exists, is constrained, funnelled through algorithmically managed forums that reward speed and superficiality over sustained inquiry. In this design, it is not the learner’s context, culture, or curiosity that shapes the learning journey; it is the logic of the platform. Algorithmic personalisation, standardised templates, and institutional branding dictate not only what is taught, but also how, why, and to whom. The result is a pedagogy of scale; that is, broad in reach but often shallow in depth, optimised for distribution, not for discovery. This is the paradox of MOOCs: they democratise access to elite content while centralising control over knowledge production. What appears open may, in practice, reinforce old hierarchies, just dressed in the aesthetics of innovation. Toward a participatory, equitable future To move beyond this constrained model, we must reimagine digital education as a relational and co-created space – one that values learning as a public good, not a product. That means shifting the paradigm from passive consumption to active participation. True openness in education requires: • Funding public, open-source digital infrastructure, including community-managed servers, multilingual content repositories, and low-bandwidth tools that serve under-connected regions. • Supporting culturally embedded content creation by local educators, using inclusive pedagogical frameworks that reflect linguistic and epistemic diversity. • Prioritising learner-led initiatives, such as peer learning networks, open badges, collaborative curriculum design, and grassroots knowledge hubs. • Embedding ethical frameworks in edtech design that centre equity, pluralism, and collective care rather than metrics and monetisation. Openness must move beyond technical access or enrolment figures. If it is to be liberatory, it must be rooted in agency, context and shared authorship. Otherwise, we risk confusing digital scale for educational justice. Conclusion: Reclaiming the meaning of openness MOOCs are not inherently harmful – but they are not inherently emancipatory either. Too often, they deliver accessibility without equity, scalability without cultural sensitivity, and instruction without participation. In doing so, they risk deepening the very inequalities they claim to address. Reclaiming openness means recentring education around human relationships, between teacher and learner, and between communities and knowledge systems. It means designing platforms that are accountable not just to venture capital or institutional prestige, but to the plural and evolving needs of learners worldwide. Openness, if it is to have any moral or pedagogical weight, must mean more than free enrolment. It must mean power shared, voices heard, and futures co-authored. James Yoonil Auh is the chair of computing and communications engineering at KyungHee Cyber University in South Korea. He has worked across the United States, Asia, and Latin America on projects linking ethics, technology, and education policy.

title: Where to next for the European Universities Initiative?
content:
Tweet
This year marks the fifth anniversary of the European Universities Initiative (EUI), one of the most ambitious and unique experiments in higher education collaboration globally.
Financed with €1.1 billion (US$1.3 billion) from 2021 to 2027, the EUI now involves over 10% of Europe’s higher education institutions – some 600 organised into 65 alliances.
The initiative was launched by the European Union to drive transformation across the sector: fostering pedagogical innovation, excellence across all university missions, institutional change, and a stronger European identity. After five years, what impact has the initiative had on Europe’s universities?
Revitalising teaching
Our research , based on semi-structured interviews with alliance participants and analyses of public documents, suggests that the EUI’s most visible impact so far has been on teaching.
This is unsurprising, given that the initiative’s funding has come largely through Erasmus+, the European Union’s programme for mobility and educational collaboration.
However, this marked the first time that the need for changing curricula to prepare and empower graduates to address the complexity of a changing world has been prioritised in a collaborative funding programme.
Our study participants described pedagogical innovation as the “heart” of their alliances and their “greatest achievement”.
Key to this transformation has been the creation of transnational communities of practice – transnational groups sustained by a shared European educational vision and a desire for inclusion and collaboration.
In each alliance, these communities have emerged as spaces where academic and administrative staff work together across borders, developing shared practices, mutual learning and collaborative innovation.
Alliances have generated a suite of new teaching activities across Europe’s universities: blended intensive programmes, hackathons, datathons, summer schools, and more.
Some are focused on internationalising existing courses to reach as many students as possible; others have developed new joint or dual degree programmes – mostly at masters level, but increasingly at bachelor degree level too.
Our study has shown that the EUI has not led to the invention of wholly new pedagogical methods or formats, but it has provided fresh frameworks and incentives for staff to think and act beyond conventional institutional structures. As one professor put it: “The alliance revitalised my teaching experience.”
The vital role of communities of practice
What has been genuinely new is the scale and complexity of the change. Typically, international elements have been integrated across dozens of courses in each institution, as, for instance, in the case of EUTOPIA .
Joint offers like summer schools or degree programmes often span entire alliances, involving 10 or more universities – and, in cases like UNA Europa or YUFE , even crossing multiple national jurisdictions for joint bachelor degrees.
This depth of collaboration has been achieved with modest funding. Despite average EU funding of just €330,000 per university per year (often supplemented by national top-ups), alliances have unlocked remarkable activity and enthusiasm, driven by a minority of committed staff within each institution.
How could an initiative with so little funding generate so much activity (and enthusiasm) among those inspired by it?
In our view, the formation of Alliances’ communities of practice (CofP) is the answer and the EUI’s core innovation. CofP have shown their potential to become the engine behind much of the initiative’s impact – sustaining new forms of collaboration, pushing pedagogical boundaries, and challenging what is traditionally valued within institutions. Yet, persistent barriers remain. The principal challenge has been that student numbers have remained low, while institutions have largely struggled to embed innovative courses and practices into their mainstream. The long-term sustainability of alliances will depend on whether universities can scale and integrate their horizontal, collaborative activities and outputs into vertical structures of workload models, reward systems and administrative processes. CofP in alliances has been anchored and sustained by a firm commitment to Europe – strengthening its values and addressing its challenges. This is a common thread through the strategic documents of alliances and in what is being heard from student representations, administrators, and (to a slightly lesser extent) academic staff. The possibility this offers is the development of a new, ‘regional’ European imaginary of higher education, one defined by collaboration, multilingualism and inclusion, alongside conventional global positioning defined by league tables. Fundamental challenges While we can explain the significant enthusiasm and activity engendered by the initiative – despite the extremely modest funding provided – we also identify three fundamental challenges. To begin with, joint research activities struggled to gain prominence in many alliance contexts equivalent to teaching. This is mainly because, through Horizon Europe, the EU already provides a strong research programme that funds international collaboration based largely on the excellence of project proposals. The sector is familiar with how to operate successfully in this space and in international research collaboration more broadly. How alliances fit into this established architecture is far from obvious. Second, the EU – the European Commission, but also its member states – embarked on the EUI knowing that it could only work with deep-seated changes in national and regional regulations that hinder collaboration in practice. The EUI needs much greater national support through overcoming red tape; this needs to be translated into universities developing more trust in each other’s processes and procedures. This points to the biggest challenges for alliances – for while innovation often happens in CofP at the institutional margins, for these practices to become sustainable, they still need to be integrated into the institutional everyday, into workloads, and into institutional systems and structures. Extra funding will help, but it will always be a tiny proportion of overall institutional income, and it is not the only resourcing needed for change. Structural issues need resolving, and they need resolving fast. Roadmap for the future So, what do our observations mean today, as the EU is finalising its proposals for a Multiannual Financial Framework, which will structure how the EU spends its money for (most likely) seven years from 2028? First, since alliances have been successful mainly through CofP, which are largely energised through bottom-up ideas about addressing common problems, it is critical that any future funding modalities the EU proposes maintain this bottom-up energy. Second, the EU must increase its spending on the alliances, starting with core business – mobility and pedagogical innovation. This must go hand-in-hand with individual countries committing to easing regulatory burdens and providing financial support. Third, such signals of support might strengthen the institutional minority active in alliances to generate more core institutional support and recognition. This must be used to ensure that the commitment of individuals in their communities of practice is based on more than mutual commitment within the group. And finally, we need more realism in the discussion about European University alliances: they are neither the panacea for ‘institutional transformation’, as the EU would like it, nor are the mobility targets to which they are committed (50% of the student population) even remotely realistic, not least because EU funding to enable this is simply not feasible. But alliances have generated unprecedented pan-European discussions, extending in many cases to global partners, about the challenges facing higher education and how to respond to these in practice. It is up to European policy-makers, but also institutions themselves, to ensure they have the will and the capacity to capitalise and build on this genuinely transnational moment in European higher education. Jan Palmowski is professor in the school of modern languages and cultures, University of Warwick, United Kingdom. Jo Angouri is professor in the department of applied linguistics, University of Warwick, UK. Their research paper, “ A paradigm shift in European transnational collaboration? ” is published in Globalisation, Societies and Education this week. This article is a commentary.
